extracted.intended_audience: writers, dramatists, actors, and general readers interested in literary and theatrical criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance and critical principles for dramatic writing, theatrical presentation, and authorial conduct — especially concerning tragic characterization, the use of stage action/show, and honesty about sources. Drawn from eighteenth-century Spectator essays addressing what makes effective and moral theatre and authorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial honesty about borrowings
rubrics_metrics.description: An author ought to 'own all that he had borrowed from others' and acknowledge translations and sources to his readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers/authors should 'lay in a clear light all that he gives his Spectators for their Money, with an Account of the first Manufacturers.' Failure to acknowledge borrowed material is compared to cheating; explicitly state when material is translated or adapted (the Spectator notes translations may 'lose much of the Majesty of the Original in the Italian').

rubrics_metrics.name: Full disclosure of exceptions and limits when offering work
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unjust to sell anything 'without telling the Exceptions against it, as well as what is to be said to its Advantage.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat literary or theatrical offerings like goods in trade: advertise both merits and limitations so purchasers/readers are not deceived. Anti-pattern: hiding faults or overstating qualities to secure applause or sales is 'no better than a Cheat.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible use of action, show, and dress
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Advantages of Action, Show, and Dress on these Occasions are allowable, because the Merit consists in being capable of imposing upon us to our Advantage and Entertainment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage spectacle and costume are justified when they help impose the piece on the audience for their benefit and entertainment. Use show to enhance, not to mask, dramatic merit; the goal is to move and please the spectator rather than merely dazzle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actor craft: manage look, voice, and gesture
rubrics_metrics.description: Speakers/actors should aim not only for 'superficial Applause' but for insinuating into the audience's affections 'by the artful Management of the Look, Voice, and Gesture of the Speaker.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directorial and acting attention should be paid to expression, emphasis, and physicality to raise terror, compassion, and other passions. Example: actors' action and emphasis can make lines 'appear decent, just, and noble' or make passions 'very artfully raised.' Anti-pattern: relying solely on words without considered physical and vocal delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid introducing absolutely faultless heroes on stage
rubrics_metrics.description: One should not introduce 'a perfect or a faultless Man upon the Stage' because 'there is no such a thing in Nature' and absolute perfection is improper to move compassion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should retain human alloy — virtues mixed with flaws — so that their misfortunes are believable and morally instructive. A fully virtuous character undermines pity and dramatic tension; even the 'most perfect Man has Vices enough to draw down Punishments.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetical justice: tragic endings for good characters are acceptable and often desirable
rubrics_metrics.description: Good men may meet with an unhappy catastrophe in tragedy; tragic endings can be 'more apt to please an Audience' and often win theatrical prizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not feel bound to show virtue rewarded on stage. Tragedies in which virtuous characters suffer can 'soften the Mind of the Beholder' and teach moral lessons by showing that prosperity is not a test of virtue. Historical/theoretical support: Aristotle noted tragedies that end unhappily often 'bore away the Prize.' Anti-pattern: forcing happy outcomes for moral neatness at the cost of naturalism and pathos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance for divergence between epic and tragic moral outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poets (e.g., Homer) often celebrate heroic success despite moral faults, whereas tragic poets may represent virtuous people as unhappy; dramatic rules need not mirror epic outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting or writing heroic material, recognize that norms for epic heroism and stage tragedy differ: an epic's triumphant hero (e.g., Achilles) can coexist with tragic representation that prefers moral complexity and suffering. Use genre-appropriate moral logic rather than applying the same rules across forms.
